objectives: Name and draw simple alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and halogenoalkanes (IUPAC) and give general formulae

blocks.title: Homologous series
blocks.md:
A **homologous series** is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula; successive members differ by CH₂. **Alkanes** C_nH₂ₙ₊₂ (single bonds); **alkenes** C_nH₂ₙ (C=C); **alcohols** C_nH₂ₙ₊₁OH (–OH); **halogenoalkanes** C_nH₂ₙ₊₁X (–Cl, –Br, –I); also carboxylic acids (–COOH), aldehydes (–CHO) and ketones (C=O) in the Upper Sixth.

The **functional group** gives the characteristic reactions. Physical properties change gradually along the series (boiling points rise with chain length).

blocks.title: IUPAC naming
blocks.md:
1. Find the **longest carbon chain** containing the functional group: meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-…
2. Number from the end that gives the **lowest number** to the functional group (then to substituents).
3. Name side groups (methyl, ethyl, chloro, bromo) as prefixes in **alphabetical order**, with locants.
4. Add the ending: -ane, -ene, -an-1-ol, etc. Example: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ = **2-methylbutane**; CH₃CH=CHCH₃ = **but-2-ene**; CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ = **propan-2-ol**.

blocks.caption: Z-but-2-ene (cis) and E-but-2-ene (trans): the methyl groups on the same side or on opposite sides of the double bond.
blocks.alt: Two drawings of but-2-ene with a double bond; in one the two methyl groups point the same way and in the other in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Isomerism
blocks.md:
**Isomers** have the same molecular formula but different structures. **Structural isomers**: *chain* (different carbon skeleton: butane and 2-methylpropane), *position* (but-1-ene and but-2-ene), *functional group* (ethanol and methoxymethane).

**E/Z isomers** need a C=C (restricted rotation) with two different groups on each carbon: **Z** if the higher-priority groups are on the same side, **E** if opposite (cis/trans for simple cases). An **optical isomer** needs a **chiral carbon** with four different groups (two mirror-image forms).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Choosing the longest chain without the functional group (the chain must include C=C or C–OH).
- Numbering from the wrong end: the functional group gets the lowest locant.
- Counting a rotated drawing as a new isomer: rotation about single bonds gives the same compound.
- Expecting E/Z isomers where one carbon of the double bond has two identical groups (propene has none).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Isomeric alkenes
blocks.statement: Draw and name the alkene isomers of C₄H₈ (open-chain).
steps: Chain length 4: but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ and but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
But-2-ene has two different groups on each double-bonded carbon, so it exists as **E** and **Z** forms.
Branched chain: 2-methylpropene (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ (no E/Z). Total: 4 alkenes (counting E and Z separately).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Isomeric alcohols
blocks.statement: Name the four alcohols with formula C₄H₁₀O and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.
steps: Straight chain: butan-1-ol (primary, OH on a CH₂ at the end) and butan-2-ol (secondary).
Branched chain: 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary: the carbon with OH bears three carbon groups).
Ethers such as ethoxyethane are further functional-group isomers but are not alcohols.

blocks.title: Alkanes
blocks.md:
Alkanes (C_nH₂ₙ₊₂) are **saturated**, with strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds: unreactive except for combustion and substitution with halogens in UV light. They are obtained from crude oil by fractional distillation; heavier fractions are **cracked** (heat/catalyst) into shorter alkanes and **alkenes**.

Complete combustion: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. In limited oxygen **carbon monoxide** (toxic: it binds to haemoglobin) or carbon (soot) forms.

blocks.title: Free-radical substitution (CH₄ + Cl₂, UV)
blocks.md:
- **Initiation**: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (homolytic fission by UV).
- **Propagation**: CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (a chain reaction).
- **Termination**: two radicals combine: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆.

A mixture of products (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄) forms because further substitution is possible.

items.text: H⁺ is attacked by the π electrons (an electrophile)

blocks.caption: Electrophilic addition of HBr to ethene through a carbocation intermediate.
blocks.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows: ethene plus hydrogen bromide, a carbocation with a bromide ion, then bromoethane.

blocks.title: Alkenes and electrophilic addition
blocks.md:
Alkenes (C_nH₂ₙ) contain a C=C: a σ bond and an electron-rich π bond that is attacked by **electrophiles** (electron-pair acceptors). Reactions: with Br₂ (the orange bromine water is **decolourised**: test for C=C), with HBr (→ bromoalkane), with steam/H₃PO₄ (→ alcohol), with H₂/Ni (→ alkane).

**Markovnikov's rule**: in the addition of HBr to propene the major product is 2-bromopropane, via the more stable (secondary) carbocation (tertiary > secondary > primary). **Addition polymerisation**: many alkene molecules join to give poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Calling alkane reactions with Cl₂ 'addition' (it is substitution via radicals).
- Drawing the curly arrow from the H–Br bond instead of from the π bond.
- Writing the monomer instead of the repeat unit in a polymer (poly(ethene) is –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ–, with no C=C).
- Using bromine water as a test with alkanes: it stays orange.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Gas volumes in combustion
blocks.statement: 20 cm³ of propane is burnt in 150 cm³ of oxygen at room conditions: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O(l). Find the gas volume after cooling.
steps: CO₂ formed = 3 × 20 = 60 cm³; O₂ used = 5 × 20 = 100 cm³.
Total gas = 60 + 50 = 110 cm³ (water is liquid and takes no volume).
blocks.answer: 110 cm³ (60 cm³ CO₂ and 50 cm³ O₂)

blocks.title: Example 2 — Markovnikov's rule
blocks.statement: Predict and explain the major product of HBr + CH₃CH=CH₂.
steps: H⁺ adds to either carbon: adding to C-1 gives CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ (secondary); adding to C-2 gives CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ (primary).
Alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon, so the secondary carbocation is more stable and is formed faster.
Br⁻ attacks it: the major product is **2-bromopropane**, CH₃CHBrCH₃.

blocks.title: Halogenoalkanes
blocks.md:
In a halogenoalkane the C–X bond is **polar** (carbon δ⁺), so it is attacked by **nucleophiles** (lone-pair donors such as OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃). **Nucleophilic substitution**: R–X + OH⁻ (aq, warm) → R–OH + X⁻ (alcohol); with KCN → nitrile (lengthens the chain); with excess NH₃ → amine.

With **ethanolic** KOH (hot), **elimination** of HX gives an alkene. Reactivity: **C–I > C–Br > C–Cl** because the bond enthalpies fall (C–Cl 346, C–Br 290, C–I 228 kJ mol⁻¹): weaker bonds break more easily.

blocks.title: Mechanisms and tests
blocks.md:
Primary halogenoalkanes react by **S_N2** (one step, nucleophile attacks as the halide leaves); tertiary ones by **S_N1** (carbocation intermediate). To identify the halogen: warm with NaOH, acidify with dilute HNO₃, add AgNO₃(aq): **AgCl white, AgBr cream, AgI yellow** precipitate.

CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) release Cl• in the upper atmosphere and destroy ozone: they are being phased out.

items.text: oxidising agent: K₂Cr₂O₇ / H⁺ (orange → green), heat

blocks.caption: Oxidation of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).
blocks.alt: A flow chart: primary alcohol to aldehyde to carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol to ketone; tertiary alcohol not oxidised.

blocks.title: Alcohols
blocks.md:
Alcohols are **primary**, **secondary** or **tertiary** depending on how many carbon groups are attached to the carbon bearing –OH. With acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (heat): primary → aldehyde (distil off) → carboxylic acid (reflux); secondary → ketone; tertiary → no reaction. The colour changes from orange to green.

**Dehydration** (conc. H₂SO₄ or hot Al₂O₃): alcohol → alkene + H₂O. **Combustion**; reaction with sodium (H₂ + sodium alkoxide); esterification with carboxylic acids (Upper Sixth).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using aqueous KOH when ethanolic KOH is needed for elimination, and vice versa.
- Adding AgNO₃ without first acidifying: hydroxide ions would give a brown precipitate of Ag₂O.
- Saying the C–F bond is the most reactive: C–F is the strongest.
- Thinking tertiary alcohols are oxidised by acidified dichromate (they are not).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Identifying a halogenoalkane
blocks.statement: A halogenoalkane is warmed with aqueous NaOH, acidified with dilute nitric acid, and silver nitrate solution is added. A cream precipitate forms. Which halogen is present, and why would the bromo compound react faster than the chloro one?
steps: A cream precipitate is silver bromide: the compound is a bromoalkane (R–Br).
Hydrolysis breaks the C–X bond; C–Br (290 kJ mol⁻¹) is weaker than C–Cl (346 kJ mol⁻¹).
So the bromoalkane reacts faster than the chloroalkane (the polarity of the bond is not the deciding factor).
blocks.answer: R–Br; the weaker C–Br bond breaks faster

blocks.title: Example 2 — Ethanol by fermentation
blocks.statement: Glucose ferments to ethanol: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ (palm sap and other sugary juices ferment in this way). Find the mass of ethanol from 180 g of glucose with a 70 % yield (A_r: C 12, H 1, O 16).
steps: M(glucose) = 180 g mol⁻¹, so n = 180/180 = 1.00 mol.
